title.rendered: The silent burden: You could be living with fibroids without knowing

content.rendered:
For almost 10 years, every menstrual cycle filled 36-year-old Funke with dread. She organised her work around her periods, never left home without extra sanitary pads and battled a constant tiredness she chalked up to the demands of her job. When her abdomen began to swell, relatives teased her, asking when she was expecting a baby.

She thought it was normal because women in her family all complained about heavy periods, so she never imagined anything was wrong. But everything changed the day she collapsed at work and was rushed to the hospital, where doctors found multiple uterine fibroids. Years of excessive menstrual bleeding had left her severely anaemic.

Funke’s story is one shared, in different ways, by millions of women across Nigeria. Many are living with fibroids without knowing it, and while some eventually get a diagnosis after years of unexplained symptoms, many more continue to suffer quietly, unaware that the pain, heavy bleeding and relentless exhaustion they’ve come to accept are actually symptoms of one of the most common gynaecological conditions affecting women.

The real tragedy isn’t just how common fibroids are; it’s that so many women have learned to live with symptoms that should have sent them to a doctor years earlier.

Fibroids are non-cancerous growths that develop in or around the uterus during a woman’s reproductive years. Although the exact cause is still unknown, hormones and genetic factors are believed to play a significant role. Women of African descent are particularly affected, and they often develop fibroids at a younger age, and the growths tend to be larger and more numerous than those seen in women of other ethnic backgrounds.

Despite how widespread the condition is, awareness remains surprisingly low. In fact, many women have no idea they are living with fibroids because the condition can remain silent for years.

Not every fibroid produces symptoms; some women discover them accidentally during routine scans, fertility investigations or pregnancy check-ups, and others only seek help after developing complications.

Even when symptoms do appear, they’re often brushed aside. Heavy menstrual bleeding is perhaps the clearest warning sign, yet many women simply accept it as part of their monthly cycle. Some have experienced excessive bleeding since adolescence and assume it’s hereditary. Others grow up believing painful periods are just something women have to endure.

The fact remains that no woman should consider severe pain or excessive bleeding normal. If your menstrual period is affecting your daily activities, causing weakness or forcing you to change your lifestyle every month, it deserves medical evaluation.

Heavy bleeding is only one of several warning signs. Fibroids can also cause prolonged menstrual periods, pelvic pain, lower abdominal swelling, frequent urination, constipation and pain during sexual intercourse. Depending on where they develop, they may interfere with conception or contribute to recurrent miscarriages.

The problem is that these symptoms usually creep up gradually. Instead of seeking medical attention, many women simply adjust their lives around them.

Unfortunately, misconceptions about menstrual health continue to stand in the way of early diagnosis. Conversations about menstruation are still considered private or even shameful, and women are more likely to discuss such issues with friends or relatives than with healthcare professionals, enabling misinformation to spread easily.

Women often try herbal remedies or resort to self-medication before seeing a qualified specialist. By the time some finally arrive at the hospital, years of heavy menstrual bleeding have left them with dangerously low blood levels.

Iron deficiency anaemia remains one of the most overlooked consequences of untreated fibroids. Continuous blood loss can leave women feeling exhausted, dizzy and short of breath. In more severe cases, emergency blood transfusions may be needed before definitive treatment can begin.

For women hoping to have children, the emotional toll can be just as devastating.

Chioma, 38, who spent years undergoing fertility treatment before doctors eventually discovered large fibroids distorting her uterus, blames herself for the information gap. When people kept asking when she would have children, she never imagined fibroids were part of the problem.

Although many women with fibroids go on to conceive naturally, specialists say some fibroids, depending on their size and location, can affect fertility or complicate pregnancy.

There are also widespread misconceptions about treatment. A common belief is that every woman diagnosed with fibroids must have surgery, but that’s simply not true. The most appropriate treatment depends on several factors, including a woman’s age, symptoms, fertility plans, and the size and location of the fibroids.

For some women, regular monitoring is all that’s required. Others benefit from medication to control heavy bleeding. Advances in minimally invasive procedures have also widened treatment options, although access to those services is still limited in many parts of Nigeria.

Another persistent myth is that pregnancy cures fibroids. While hormonal changes during pregnancy can affect their size, fibroids may continue to grow and, in some cases, complicate both pregnancy and childbirth.

Postponing medical care in the hope that pregnancy will make the fibroids disappear may expose women to unnecessary risks. Awareness remains one of the strongest tools for reducing the burden. Women who experience unusually heavy menstrual bleeding, prolonged periods, persistent pelvic pain, abdominal swelling or unexplained fatigue should seek medical attention without delay. In most cases, a pelvic examination followed by an ultrasound scan is enough to confirm the diagnosis before complications arise.

Routine gynaecological check-ups are equally important, particularly for women with a family history of fibroids or previous reproductive challenges. Beyond diagnosis and treatment, experts say society must also rethink the way it responds to women’s reproductive health concerns.

Too often, women’s pain is minimised or dismissed as simply part of being female. As a result, many continue to suffer in silence, afraid of being judged, misunderstood or told to endure what they’re experiencing. That silence comes at a price.

For many women, an early diagnosis could have spared years of pain, severe anaemia and emotional distress. It is important to pay attention to what your body is telling you. Speak to a doctor much earlier, and not spend years believing that you just have difficult periods. If you look back, you will realise that your body had been warning you all along. Fibroids don’t always make a dramatic entrance; sometimes they reveal themselves through heavier periods, lingering fatigue or a gradually enlarging abdomen. Recognising these early signs and seeking help promptly can make all the difference, preventing years of unnecessary suffering and opening the door to timely treatment.
